text: Everything a neural network does is arithmetic on numbers, and a sentence is not a number. So before a language model can read a single word, the text has to be cut into pieces, and every piece has to be given a number. Those pieces are called tokens, and the choice of how to cut turns out to shape almost everything that comes after.

The simplest cut is one token per character. We collect every distinct character that appears in the text, sort them, and give each one an index, much like numbering the seats in a small theatre so that every guest has a fixed place. The word hello then becomes a short list of seat numbers, and decoding is just reading the seats back. The vocabulary is tiny, which is pleasant, but every sentence becomes a very long sequence, and the model has to spend its effort learning to spell before it can learn what words mean.

The opposite cut gives every whole word its own token. Sequences become short, because one token now carries a lot of meaning, but the vocabulary explodes, since every tense, plural and misspelling needs a seat of its own. Worse, a word the model never saw during training has no seat at all, and it can only be replaced by a placeholder that means unknown, which throws its meaning away.

The method most language models use sits between these two, and it is called byte pair encoding. It starts from single characters, counts every pair of neighbouring tokens in a large body of text, and takes the most frequent pair, which here is the letter t followed by the letter h. That pair is fused into a brand new token, every occurrence is rewritten, and the counting starts again. It works the way a stenographer invents shorthand: the combinations she writes most often earn a symbol of their own.

Repeat the merge many thousands of times and something useful emerges. Common words end up as a single token, while a rare word is spelled out of a few familiar pieces, so nothing is ever truly unknown. Modern tokenizers go one step further and start from raw bytes instead of characters, so that any text at all, including accents and emoji, can be written with the starting pieces.

Notice that a token's number is only a name tag. Token five hundred is not larger than token seven in any meaningful sense, so the model cannot do useful arithmetic on the identifiers themselves. What it needs instead is a rich list of numbers for every token, a vector that can carry meaning, and that is the subject of the next lesson, on embeddings.
